actions.justification: Mandatory first step: patient is tachycardic with hematemesis/melena and cirrhosis — hemodynamic status must be assessed immediately to determine shock and resuscitation needs.
Mandatory: full vital sign assessment is required to characterize the severity of bleeding and guide resuscitation in this acute upper GI bleed.
Mandatory: large-bore IV access is essential for fluid resuscitation and medication administration in active GI bleeding.
Mandatory. CBC to assess hemoglobin, hematocrit, and platelet count — critical for evaluating degree of blood loss and guiding transfusion decisions in this patient with active GI bleeding.
Mandatory. Cirrhosis commonly causes coagulopathy; PT/INR assessment is essential before any procedural intervention and to guide FFP/vitamin K administration.
Mandatory. Type and crossmatch required to prepare packed RBCs for potential transfusion given active hematemesis and melena with tachycardia.

Patient has cirrhosis with hematemesis/melena — high suspicion for variceal bleeding. Octreotide (somatostatin analogue) reduces portal pressure and splanchnic blood flow and should be initiated early in suspected variceal GI bleeding per AASLD/ACG guidelines.

Urgent GI consultation is indicated for upper GI bleeding in a cirrhotic patient. Early endoscopy (within 12 hours) is guideline-recommended for diagnosis and therapeutic intervention (band ligation or sclerotherapy for varices).
BMP is needed to assess renal function (hepatorenal syndrome risk in cirrhosis), electrolytes, and BUN/creatinine ratio to support upper GI bleed diagnosis and guide fluid/transfusion management.

IV PPI (proton pump inhibitor) is indicated for upper GI bleeding to reduce acid exposure and stabilize clots. Patient has hematemesis and melena with cirrhosis — PPI is standard of care alongside octreotide (already given).

Prokinetic agents (e.g., erythromycin) given before endoscopy improve gastric emptying and visualization of the bleeding source, which is important for this patient with hematemesis prior to planned endoscopy.

Lactate assessment helps evaluate tissue perfusion and occult shock. Despite relatively stable BP, HR of 105 with GI bleeding in a cirrhotic patient warrants lactate to detect early hemodynamic compromise.
Patient with cirrhosis and active GI bleeding (hematemesis/melena) needs type and crossmatch to prepare for potential packed RBC transfusion. This is critical for hemorrhage management.
HR 105 with active upper GI bleeding suggests hemodynamic compromise. IV crystalloid bolus supports perfusion while awaiting blood products and definitive hemostasis.

CT abdomen can help identify bleeding source and assess for complications in this cirrhotic patient with active GI hemorrhage, especially if endoscopy is being planned or to evaluate for portal hypertension complications.

Initial CBC was ordered but is pending at 75 minutes. Repeating/following up on CBC is critical to assess hemoglobin level and guide transfusion decisions in this cirrhotic patient with active upper GI bleeding (hematemesis/melena).

Patient has cirrhosis with active GI bleeding. Evidence-based guidelines recommend restrictive transfusion strategy with threshold of Hgb <7 g/dL in cirrhotic patients with upper GI bleeding. This conditional order should be placed while awaiting CBC results.

Patient with cirrhosis, hematemesis, and melena may have variceal or non-variceal bleeding requiring surgical backup. Surgical consultation is appropriate given the severity of presentation and in case endoscopic or pharmacologic management fails.

Patient with hematemesis/melena and cirrhosis has HR 105 suggesting ongoing hemodynamic stress. Repeat lactate helps assess tissue perfusion and adequacy of resuscitation after IV fluids and packed RBCs given earlier.
Repeat CBC to trend hemoglobin/hematocrit and assess response to transfusion therapy in this GI bleeding patient, guiding need for further blood product administration.

Patient with cirrhosis presenting with hematemesis and melena with persistent tachycardia (HR 105) despite initial resuscitation measures. Angiography may be indicated to evaluate and potentially treat the source of GI bleeding, particularly if variceal or other vascular source is suspected and endoscopic therapy is being considered or has failed. This is the only available action in the current phase.
